agent_notes: STEPBible glosses אֱלֹהֵינוּ with the entity deity.yhwh and the word as 'God our'; I kept 'our God'. הַמַּגְבִּיהִי and its parallel הַמַּשְׁפִּילִי carry a superfluous yod (hireq-yod) that is a poetic archaic ending, not a first-person suffix. Rashi on Ps 113:5 and Metzudat Zion list it with מקימי, להושיבי, מושיבי. Ibn Ezra on Ps 113:5 reports a view that the construction is 'who makes his glory high'; I follow his own reading, 'as it sounds'.

הַמַּשְׁפִּילִי לִרְאוֹת is ambiguous: 'who stoops to see' (reflexive sense, KJV, YLT 'humbling Himself') or 'who brings low in order to see'. I followed the majority and Metzudat David (he lowers his gaze), and rendered the literal layer as 'who makes low to see', which keeps both open.

The packet's STEPBible morph for אַשְׁפֹּת is singular; Radak and Ibn Ezra on Ps 113:7 say the form is singular, so I did not render it as a plural 'heaps'. 'Ash heap' rather than KJV 'dunghill' is my choice; Metzudat Zion glosses it as dung and refuse (דומן וזבל), so the dung sense is real and I mention it in the commentary.

agent_notes: עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת: Radak and Meiri say עקרת is the absolute form (as עקרה), so 'barren woman of the house' is a construct reading that Radak rejects and Ibn Ezra rejects too (the word is not in construct with הבית). The literal layer therefore reads 'the barren woman [in] the house', with the house as the place she is seated. KJV 'keep house' is therefore a paraphrase of the sitting verb. The reading in the Targum, 'the assembly of Israel', is allegorical and I only mention it.

Malbim's claim that the barren wife drank a 'cup of barrenness' (so the household had a second wife kept for beauty) is a rabbinic-period custom (cf. the Talmudic discussion of כוס עקרים); I cite Malbim only for his own statement and do not present it as the practice of the psalmist's day.
